units.title: Define occlusion
units.lesson: Occlusion describes how upper and lower teeth meet. It concerns relationships, not simply whether individual teeth look straight. A visible alignment description and a bite relationship answer different questions. Start a structured orthodontic description by using the correct anatomical terms, while recognizing that assessment also considers function and wider facial relationships.
units.question: What does occlusion describe?
choices: How upper and lower teeth meet
units.explanation: Occlusion concerns the relationship between upper and lower teeth.
rationales: Restoration count does not define occlusion.

units.title: Describe the mismatch
units.lesson: Malocclusion means an abnormal fit between upper and lower teeth. Open bite describes a lack of contact in a region when other teeth are together. Overjet concerns the forward relationship of upper incisors to lower incisors. Avoid confusing a horizontal relationship with vertical overlap. These descriptions are not a treatment prescription or a full skeletal diagnosis.
units.question: Which term concerns forward projection of upper incisors relative to lower incisors?
units.explanation: Overjet describes a horizontal incisor relationship.
rationales: The pulp chamber is internal anatomy.

units.title: Recognize a developmental stage
units.lesson: Mixed dentition means primary and permanent teeth are present together. It is a developmental stage, not a disease. Chronological ages are approximate and individual timing varies. Describe the teeth actually present rather than assuming every child of a given age has the identical stage or eruption pattern.
units.question: Which combination defines mixed dentition?
units.explanation: The coexistence of primary and permanent teeth defines the term.
rationales: This is not the developmental combination.

units.title: Understand why retention follows movement
units.lesson: After active orthodontic treatment, teeth can change position. Retainers help maintain the achieved alignment. The retention phase is therefore part of maintaining a result, rather than evidence that active movement has never occurred. Appliance choice and wearing instructions are individualized; this chapter does not prescribe a schedule.
units.question: What is the main purpose of orthodontic retention?
units.explanation: Retention helps preserve the result after active movement.
rationales: This is the purpose of a retainer.
Tooth replacement is a different role.
